g: Narrative nonfiction; science, medicine and family history
sum: In 1951 doctors at Johns Hopkins took cells from Henrietta Lacks, a young Black mother dying of cervical cancer, without her knowledge. Her cells, named HeLa, became the first human cells to grow indefinitely in a laboratory and fuelled polio vaccines, cancer research and countless discoveries. Rebecca Skloot tells that story alongside the Lacks family’s, who did not learn of it for decades.
bg: Published in 2010 after more than a decade of research, the book became a long-running bestseller and was adapted into a 2017 television film starring Oprah Winfrey. Skloot set up a foundation to support Lacks family members and others affected by research without consent.
br: The book moves between three timelines: Henrietta’s life and death, the science and business of HeLa, and Skloot’s relationship with the family, especially Henrietta’s daughter Deborah. Short chapters keep the threads moving.
la: Skloot uses immersive journalism, placing herself in the story and giving family members’ voices and dialect space on the page, so the reader feels the human cost behind the scientific triumph.
cx: The story raises lasting questions about informed consent, race and medical research, and the commercial use of human tissue. The Lacks estate reached a settlement with a biotech company over HeLa in 2023.
th: Consent and ownership
Who owns our cells, our tissue and our medical data?
Race and medicine
Black patients were exploited and excluded by medical institutions.
Family and memory
The family’s grief, confusion and pride over HeLa shape the story.
fit: Pairs science with history and ethics, alongside The Emperor of All Maladies and The Gene already on your list.
mis: Some readers question the author’s prominent role in the family’s story, and the dual focus can feel uneven.
rq: What did Henrietta’s family lose, and what did they gain?
How did HeLa change medical science?
How does Skloot handle her own role?
dq: Should patients share in profits from their tissue?
What would justice look like for the Lacks family?

sum: Oliver Sacks presents patients whose neurological conditions alter perception, memory and identity: a music teacher who cannot recognise faces and mistakes his wife for a hat, a former sailor who believes it is still 1945, twins who exchange enormous prime numbers for fun. Each case becomes a meditation on what it means to be a self, and how people adapt to profound loss.
bg: Published in 1985, the collection made Sacks, a British neurologist practising in New York, one of the best-known science writers in the world. Several cases inspired plays, an opera and later works by other writers. Sacks died in 2015.
br: Each case is short and self-contained, so read a few at a time. The four sections, on losses, excesses, transports and the world of the simple, frame the cases in different ways.
la: Sacks writes clinical tales in the tradition of nineteenth-century case histories, combining precise medical detail with deep empathy, literary allusion and philosophical speculation. He is always curious about what each patient can still do, not only what has been lost.
cx: Later critics have raised questions about consent, privacy and how some disabled people are framed in the cases. Sacks’ language reflects the 1980s, and he himself revisited his approach in later work.
th: Identity and the brain
Who we are depends on fragile and surprising neural processes.
Adaptation
Patients find remarkable ways to live with profound neurological loss.
Medicine as storytelling
Understanding a patient requires listening to their story.
fit: Bridges psychology and literature; pairs with Hallucinations and with Behave on your list.
mis: Some terminology and framing feel dated, and ethical questions about writing about patients remain.
rq: Which patient’s story stayed with you longest?
How does Sacks balance science and compassion?
What do these cases reveal about memory?
dq: What are the ethics of writing about patients?
Has reading this changed your idea of the self?

sum: Oliver Sacks explores hallucinations of many kinds: those caused by failing eyesight or hearing, migraine, epilepsy, Parkinson’s disease, fever, drugs, grief, and the edges of sleep. He argues that hallucinations are far more common than we think, are often not a sign of madness at all, and reveal how the brain constructs the experience we take for reality.
bg: Published in 2012, late in Sacks’ career, the book includes candid accounts of his own extensive drug experiments as a young doctor in California in the 1960s, which he had not written about publicly before. He was nearly eighty when it appeared.
br: Chapters are organised by cause rather than chronology, so you can dip in where curious. The chapter on Charles Bonnet syndrome, hallucinations in people losing their sight, makes a good starting point.
la: Sacks blends patient letters and accounts, historical and literary sources, and his own experience, with characteristic warmth, curiosity and digressive footnotes. The tone is gentle and unsensational, even when the experiences described are frightening.
cx: Part of the book’s purpose is to destigmatise hallucinations, which many people hide for fear of being thought mentally ill, and to show their role in religious and artistic experience.
th: Perception as construction
The brain fills in what it expects to see, hear and feel.
Destigmatising experience
Hallucinations are common and varied, and are rarely a sign of madness.
Self-experiment
Sacks turns his own past drug use into evidence and honest reflection.
fit: A companion to The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat, and a link to the psychology and neuroscience on your list.
mis: It is episodic and anecdotal, with less narrative drive than a single story, and can feel like a catalogue.
rq: Which kind of hallucination surprised you most?
How does the brain construct perception?
How does Sacks use his own story?
dq: Should hallucinations always be treated as symptoms?
What do they suggest about the nature of reality?

g: Narrative nonfiction; history of psychology and behavioural economics
sum: Michael Lewis tells the story of the friendship between Israeli psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, whose experiments on judgment, probability and bias overturned the assumption that people make decisions rationally. Their intense partnership, with its creative highs, its jealousy and its eventual strains, drives the book as much as the ideas.
bg: Published in 2016 by the author of Moneyball and The Big Short. Lewis has said a review of Moneyball pointed out that the real story behind it was Kahneman and Tversky’s work, which led him to write this book.
br: Read alongside or after Thinking, Fast and Slow; Lewis supplies the human story behind the concepts. The opening chapter on basketball scouting is a prologue, and the main story begins after it.
la: Lewis writes character-driven narrative, using vivid scenes, letters and the dynamics of the friendship to explain heuristics and biases without formulas. Dialogue and personal detail make abstract findings feel like discoveries made by real people.
cx: The story spans Israeli wars, academic life in Jerusalem and North America, and the rise of behavioural economics. Kahneman received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics in 2002, six years after Tversky’s death.
th: Collaboration
Great ideas can come from two minds thinking as one.
Intuition’s errors
Human judgment is systematically and predictably biased in specific ways.
Credit and recognition
Unequal fame can strain even the closest partnership.
fit: A narrative companion to Thinking, Fast and Slow and Noise, both connected to this book on your list.
mis: Lighter on the science than the original works, and the opening detour may frustrate readers eager to get to the main story.
rq: What made the partnership work so well?
Which bias do you recognise in yourself?
How did their personalities shape their research?
dq: Can creative partnerships ever be truly equal?
How has behavioural economics changed public policy?

sum: Julia Galef contrasts the soldier mindset, which defends what we already believe, with the scout mindset, which wants to see things as they actually are, even when the truth is unwelcome. She argues that accuracy can be compatible with happiness, confidence and motivation, and offers practical tests for noticing when we are deceiving ourselves.
bg: Published in 2021 by the co-founder of the Center for Applied Rationality and long-time host of the podcast Rationally Speaking. Galef draws on psychology research and on examples from science, business, activism and personal life. Her TED talk on the topic preceded the book.
br: Short and practical: try the self-tests as you read, such as imagining the same evidence supporting the other side. It works well as a follow-up to the heavier bias research on your list.
la: Galef writes clearly and fairly, with an even, friendly tone, using memorable examples rather than relying only on laboratory studies, and anticipating objections to her own argument. Charts and short exercises break up the argument.
cx: The book is part of a wave of popular works on reasoning and decision-making influenced by Kahneman’s research and by the online rationalist community. It is notably less pessimistic than most bias literature.
th: Motivated reasoning
We defend beliefs for comfort, belonging and self-image.
Calibration
Good thinkers know how sure they actually should be.
Holding identity lightly
Keeping beliefs separate from identity makes it easier to change your mind.
fit: A practical, optimistic complement to the bias research on your list, easy to apply in daily life.
mis: It can feel simple or self-help-ish next to academic psychology, and some examples are familiar.
rq: Where do you tend to use soldier mindset?
What would holding your identity lightly mean for you?
dq: Could a whole society adopt a scout mindset?
